identifications.body:
jlboyer, as objective as I can be ( since I created The Green Hairstreak Corridor) a couple of things for folks here at iNat: a) it's not Endangered, though the experience of seeing them is becoming rarer for most San Franciscans and b) The International Tribunal for Zoological Nomenclature 
(ITZN) has reverted to a prior Latin name for the "Coastal" Green Hairstreak: Callophyrs viridis. The "Bramble" Green Hairstreak is now C. dumertorum.
Confusing and iNat will no doubt catch up to this soon. Fantastic picture...but I'm partial to this creature.

non_owner_ids.body:
jlboyer, as objective as I can be ( since I created The Green Hairstreak Corridor) a couple of things for folks here at iNat: a) it's not Endangered, though the experience of seeing them is becoming rarer for most San Franciscans and b) The International Tribunal for Zoological Nomenclature 
(ITZN) has reverted to a prior Latin name for the "Coastal" Green Hairstreak: Callophyrs viridis. The "Bramble" Green Hairstreak is now C. dumertorum.
Confusing and iNat will no doubt catch up to this soon. Fantastic picture...but I'm partial to this creature.

description: Bad photo, but the ID is good. There were 2 individuals dancing through the buckwheat at Wherry Corridor, a recently restored dune scrub site. It is the beginning of the second growing season at this site since removal of 20-plus cypress and pine. Immediately following tree removal, the sand was inverted using a large excavator. The success of dune annuals continues this year, and the appearance of the hairstreak is as gratifying as the sight of thousands of native dune annual seedlings--despite the drought. I believe this is the furthest east we have observed the green hairstreak in the Presidio, as it expands its range following habitat restoration.

Callophrys rubi is a European species, please don't use this one for American hairstreaks.

I'm sure it was just a mistake based on the common name. Prakrit, if you can update your identification and/or opt-in to the community ID for this one this observation will appear with the other C. viridis observations.
Yes sorry if I sounded blunt.

comments.body: Oh, OK! Thanks.
Tom, I don't know why, but the map for your sighting places it in Daly City, not San Francisco!

This species is "imperiled" according to NatureServe, so we obscure coordinates of its observations. When you see that big circle on the map it means it the observation is somewhere within the circle.

place_guess: Rocky Outcrop Park, San Francisco, California, United States

Looks like you and dpom have different IDs for the same butterfly:
http://www.inaturalist.org/observations/660440
We need robberfly to settle this.
It's a horrifying tale of taxonomic woe: checkout these two swaps.

description:
Saw four today all hill-topping on Rocky Outcrop. This incredibly-fresh one sitting on it's host: Erigonum latifolium ( Coast Buckwheat ) The teal blue/green color at the base thorax of each wing is only present for it's first few days of flight - it wears off and becomes uniformly green.
This site is part of a project I created awhile back:
http://www.sfbutterfly.com/www.sfbutterfly.com/Green_Hairstreak.html

identifications.body:
Welcome to the quagmire that is the "Green Hairstreak complex". The Presidio/Upper Sunset populations remaining in SF County show distinct signs of having once supported both species. It's now all treated as C. viridis ( Coastal Green ) - that only happened last year. Put  your seatbelts on for this part : Coastal Green used to be C. dumetorum. They reverted C. dumertorum to C. viridis AND THEN bumped C. dumetorum to Bramble. 
With regards to mapping, perhaps @loarie to address why all Green Hairstreak postings are obscured on INat @kueda ? It confuses me.

comments.body: @nlblock Thank you for helping to identify this individual!  I apologize for the blurry picture, although you can still make out a white curve pattern formed by the white underwing markings, which is consistent with Callophrys viridis.  To the best of my limited knowledge, C. dumetorum has never been recorded in San Francisco (it doesn't mean they can't be here).
I hadn't realized that dumetorum was not found locally! Sorry about that. Does viridis show such extensive brown on the forewing? I always thought that was a dumetorum field mark. @robberfly
Was this seen on San Bruno?
@robberfly this individual was observed below Inspiration Point in the Presidio.

identifications.body: White dots on hind wing. That brown, triangle notch on the ventral forewing is normally indicative of C. dumetorum, however populations of both species in SF Co. & San Bruno Mountain can have this - which shows really it’s more of a complex. A location is helpful in keying one away from the other. Unfortunately these creatures are called “endangered” on iNat ( which they’re not ) and all are automatically obscured.

comments.body: @robberfly Ah, the white dots! Thank you. Do you recognize this individual from a week ago, or can you tell its age from the wear on its wings (or something else entirely)?

It’s worn status: one learns to recognized a fresh individual: not a scale missing And an individual on-the-wing a few days: birdstreaks and worn wings. It’s a party trick all Naturalists can learn. Stick with it...your on your way, my friend...:/
@robberfly I was out there again today and noticed a bit more nuance in the scales. Thank you for the attention-narrowing tip!

comments.body: Wow, that's really stunning
I agree! I had a question— what trail should I look for the San Bruno Elfin on? I was on there on Sunday, but I think I was in the wrong spot.

If you go on a weekend, drive up to the parking lot on the top of the ridge, park here and walk back along the west side of the road. There is one concentration of them a few hillcuts down to about the intersection with summit Trail. You could also take Summit Trail down to the Ridge Trail and/or Dairy Ravine Trail. I've had the elfins along those trails too in smaller numbers
Awesome, thanks so much for the tips!!! I was mostly along the dairy ravine trail, so I only got fleeting glances of one candidate. When do you think is the latest time of year to go and see these?
I'd guess you have about 2-3 weeks left at most so mid-April at the very latest. San Bruno Elfin are single brooded. Majority of sightings seem to be from March 10th through the end of the month.
Ok perfect, thanks for the tips.
